title: Stage 2 – Create three network namespaces (host1, router, host2)
cmd: sudo ip netns add host1; sudo ip netns add router; sudo ip netns add host2
note: Three isolated network namespaces act as host1, router and host2.

title: Stage 2 – Verify namespaces
cmd: sudo ip netns list
note: host1, router and host2 are listed.

title: Stage 2 – Create virtual cables (veth pairs)
cmd: sudo ip link add veth-h1 type veth peer name veth-r1; sudo ip link add veth-r2 type veth peer name veth-h2; echo done
note: Two virtual Ethernet cables: host1<->router and router<->host2.

title: Stage 2 – Plug cables into the namespaces
cmd: sudo ip link set veth-h1 netns host1; sudo ip link set veth-r1 netns router; sudo ip link set veth-r2 netns router; sudo ip link set veth-h2 netns host2; echo done
note: Each end of each cable is moved into its namespace.

title: Stage 3 – Configure IP addresses on host1
cmd: sudo ip netns exec host1 ip addr add 10.0.1.1/30 dev veth-h1; sudo ip netns exec host1 ip link set veth-h1 up; sudo ip netns exec host1 ip link set lo up; sudo ip netns exec host1 ip -br addr
note: host1 = 10.0.1.1/30 (last command shows the result).

title: Stage 3 – Configure IP addresses on router
cmd: sudo ip netns exec router ip addr add 10.0.1.2/30 dev veth-r1; sudo ip netns exec router ip addr add 10.0.2.1/30 dev veth-r2; sudo ip netns exec router ip link set veth-r1 up; sudo ip netns exec router ip link set veth-r2 up; sudo ip netns exec router ip link set lo up; sudo ip netns exec router ip -br addr

title: Stage 3 – Configure IP addresses on host2
cmd: sudo ip netns exec host2 ip addr add 10.0.2.2/30 dev veth-h2; sudo ip netns exec host2 ip link set veth-h2 up; sudo ip netns exec host2 ip link set lo up; sudo ip netns exec host2 ip -br addr

title: Stage 4 – Enable routing

title: Stage 6 – Add 20 ms delay and 1% loss on router veth-r2
cmd: sudo ip netns exec router tc qdisc add dev veth-r2 root netem delay 20ms loss 1%

title: Stage 12 (extra) – Give the capture files to the current user

title: Stage 13 – Check TTL at point 1 (host1, cap1)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap1.pcap -T fields -e ip.ttl -Y "ip" 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c
note: Packets leaving host1 have TTL 64; replies coming back from host2 have already crossed the router, so they show TTL 63.

title: Stage 13 – Check TTL at point 2 (router, cap2)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap2.pcap -T fields -e ip.ttl -Y "ip" 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c
note: At the router's host1-side interface: TTL 64 (from host1) and 63 (replies already forwarded by the router).

title: Stage 13 – Check TTL at point 3 (host2, cap3)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap3.pcap -T fields -e ip.ttl -Y "ip" 2>/dev/null | sort | uniq -c
note: Packets from host1 arrive at host2 with TTL 63: the router decremented the TTL by 1. Replies originated by host2 leave with TTL 64.

title: Stage 14 – Read the actual message from the router capture (data.text)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap2.pcap -Y "tcp.port == 1234" -T fields -e data.text 2>/dev/null
note: The plain-text message is visible in the packets captured at the router.

title: Read message as hex/ASCII from the router capture (xxd)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap2.pcap -Y "tcp.port == 1234" -T fields -e tcp.payload 2>/dev/null | xxd | head -20
note: Hex dump of the TCP payload bytes (the text is sent unencrypted).

title: Check delay – SYN time in cap1 (host1)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap1.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e frame.time_relative 2>/dev/null
note: Relative time of the first SYN in each capture (each file starts at its own first packet, so it is 0 in all three).

title: Check delay – SYN time in cap2 (router)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap2.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e frame.time_relative 2>/dev/null
note: Same measurement at the router.

title: Check delay – SYN time in cap3 (host2)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap3.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e frame.time_relative 2>/dev/null
note: Same measurement at host2.

title: Check delay using absolute (epoch) timestamps – cap1 vs cap3
cmd: for c in 1 2 3; do printf "cap$c SYN epoch time: "; tshark -r /tmp/cap$c.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e frame.time_epoch 2>/dev/null; done
note: Additional step: absolute time stamps are needed to compare points; the difference between cap1 and cap3 shows the delay added by the router (~20 ms netem delay).
output:
cap1 SYN epoch time: 1795080100.354231611
cap2 SYN epoch time: 1795080100.354249026
cap3 SYN epoch time: 1795080100.374382231

title: Check delay – difference cap3 − cap1 in milliseconds
cmd: a=$(tshark -r /tmp/cap1.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e frame.time_epoch 2>/dev/null); b=$(tshark -r /tmp/cap3.pcap -Y "tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0" -T fields -e frame.time_epoch 2>/dev/null); echo "cap1 = $a"; echo "cap3 = $b"; python3 -c "print('difference =', round((float('$b')-float('$a'))*1000,2), 'ms')"
note: Difference between cap1 and cap3 is approximately 20 ms, as expected.

title: Check retransmissions in cap1
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap1.pcap -Y "tcp.analysis.retransmission" 2>/dev/null | wc -l
note: Number of TCP retransmissions seen at this point. With only about 18 packets and 1% loss, a drop is unlikely, so 0 is a plausible honest result.

title: Check retransmissions in cap2
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap2.pcap -Y "tcp.analysis.retransmission" 2>/dev/null | wc -l
note: Number of TCP retransmissions seen at this point. With only about 18 packets and 1% loss, a drop is unlikely, so 0 is a plausible honest result.

title: Check retransmissions in cap3
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap3.pcap -Y "tcp.analysis.retransmission" 2>/dev/null | wc -l
note: Number of TCP retransmissions seen at this point. With only about 18 packets and 1% loss, a drop is unlikely, so 0 is a plausible honest result.

title: Check RTT with mtr
cmd: sudo ip netns exec host1 mtr --report 10.0.2.2
note: Per-hop latency report from host1 through the router to host2 (~20 ms at the last hop because of netem).

title: Read message text from the router capture – decoded payload (extra)
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/cap2.pcap -Y "tcp.port == 1234 && tcp.len > 0" -T fields -e tcp.payload 2>/dev/null | xxd -r -p
note: Extra step: the data.text field was empty on this tshark version, so the hex payload is decoded back to text. The messages typed on host1 are readable at the router.

title: Wireshark step – merge all 3 captures (File > Merge equivalent)
cmd: mergecap -w /tmp/merged.pcap /tmp/cap1.pcap /tmp/cap2.pcap /tmp/cap3.pcap; capinfos -c /tmp/merged.pcap
note: mergecap does the same as File > Merge in Wireshark: all three capture points in one file.

title: Wireshark step – TTL column (Custom column ip.ttl) for the message packets
cmd: tshark -r /tmp/merged.pcap -Y "tcp.port == 1234" -T fields -e frame.number -e frame.time_epoch -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e ip.ttl -e tcp.flags.str -e tcp.len 2>/dev/null | sort -k2 | head -40
note: Same as adding a TTL column in Wireshark. TTL 64 at points 1 and 2 on packets sent by host1; TTL 63 on those packets as seen at point 3 (host2).
